Reinforcement learning for optical impairment correction

A bandit proof of concept found useful equalizer coefficients in roughly 1,000 rounds and motivated a more scalable Q-learning formulation.

At a glance

Turn equalizer search into sequential decision-making.

UCBQ-learningPMDAdaptive filters
Problem

A 2×2 polarization equalizer contains many coupled complex coefficients. Even a heavily discretized toy version produces 3¹²—more than 531,000—possible filter combinations, making exhaustive evaluation impractical.

Bandit proof of concept

Coefficient sets are treated as arms and negative CMA error as reward. UCB balances exploration and exploitation, locating the strongest tested set in roughly 1,000 rounds for the compact case.

Scaling with Q-learning

Instead of selecting a complete filter independently, the state represents current coefficients while actions increment, decrement, or retain each coefficient in turn. This reduces the decision to 72 local actions and creates a path toward experience replay or a deep Q-network.

Takeaway

The useful shift is from choosing among every possible equalizer to learning how to navigate coefficient space. The project also makes explicit where a naive action space breaks down.
